summary.text: A core sample is a cylinder cut from a material such as sediment or rock, usually by drilling with a hollow steel tube called a core drill.
The sample is pushed more or less intact into the tube, then removed in the laboratory and analyzed with methods chosen for the data wanted.
A core loses much of its value if its context is lost, so the borehole, its position and which way is up must stay recorded with it.

facts.label: Deepest sources
facts.value: Over 10 km below Earth's surface in a borehole

facts.label: Diameter range
facts.value: A few millimeters to over 150 millimeters

facts.label: Hand corer reach
facts.value: Decimeters in clay to meters in lake sediment

items.prompt: A sampler is simply dropped into the soft mud of a lake bed. Why do cores taken this way have to stay relatively small?

options.label: Lake water dissolves any larger core
The weak mud limits the core's size
Large tubes float instead of sinking
Labs cannot store anything bigger

items.explain: In gravity coring, the low strength of the material being penetrated means the cores have to be relatively small.

items.prompt: A core reaches the lab with no note of which hole it came from or which end was up. What is the main problem?

options.label: It must be drilled again from the same spot
Its age can still be read from its chemistry
It will decay faster without a label
It loses much of its worth for good

items.explain: A core that cannot be related to its original context has lost much of its benefit, and once that data is separated it is generally impossible to regain.

items.prompt: Why do scientists coring a tree to date its rings try to include the bark in the sample?

options.label: To pin down the date of the latest growth
To keep the core from drying and cracking
To measure how thick the trunk is
To stop the tree from becoming infected

items.explain: Including a bark surface lets the date of the tree's most recent growth be determined without doubt.

items.prompt: A student with a hand-held corer wants mud from 30 meters down in a lake bed. What is the catch?

options.label: Hand corers only work on dry land
Hand corers cost more than drill rigs
Hand corers reach only a few meters at most
Hand corers melt the mud as they cut

items.explain: Coring by hand is cheap and quick but reaches only limited depths, from a few decimeters in clay to a few meters in soft lake sediment.

items.prompt: Small cores are fired into the wall of a borehole with explosive 'bullets'. Why are they doubtful for measuring porosity?

options.label: They are too long to fit in a lab
They tend to come out badly shattered
They are always taken from the wrong rock
They soak up too much drilling fluid

items.explain: Percussion sidewall cores tend to be heavily shattered, which makes porosity and permeability measurements dubious.

items.prompt: Coring teams now take more care to stop cores being damaged on their way to and through the lab. What is the usual method?

options.label: Freezing them solid with liquid nitrogen
Baking them dry in a hot oven
Storing them under running water
Slicing them into thin sheets at once

items.explain: The usual way to prevent damage is to freeze the core completely using liquid nitrogen, which is cheap to obtain.
